description: Functionalist, Marxist, feminist and New Right theories of the family’s role in society.
content_html:
The Conflict versus Consensus Debate

One of the defining debates in GCSE Sociology is between consensus perspectives, which argue that social institutions like the family benefit society as a whole, and conflict perspectives, which argue that the family primarily serves the interests of powerful groups at the expense of others. Functionalism represents the consensus view; Marxism, feminism and the New Right each offer different conflict analyses. Understanding this debate — and being able to present each perspective with named sociologists — is central to the families unit.

Functionalist Theory of the Family: Parsons

Talcott Parsons argued that in modern industrial societies the family performs two irreducible functions that no other institution can perform as effectively. First, the primary socialisation of children — instilling the shared norms and values that allow individuals to participate in society. Second, the stabilisation of adult personalities. Parsons described this as the “warm bath” effect: the family provides emotional comfort and psychological stability for adult members, releasing the tensions that accumulate in the competitive world of paid work.

Parsons argued that the instrumental role (performed by the husband/father — breadwinner, financial provider) and the expressive role (performed by the wife/mother — emotional nurturer, homemaker) are biologically grounded and functionally necessary. He presented these as complementary: different but equally important. From a functionalist perspective, the nuclear family with gender-divided roles is the most efficient unit for meeting society’s needs.

Key Fact

Parsons argued the family has two irreducible functions: (1) primary socialisation — teaching children the norms and values needed to participate in society; (2) stabilisation of adult personalities — the “warm bath” of emotional comfort that releases tensions from paid work. The instrumental role (breadwinner) is performed by the male partner; the expressive role (emotional carer) is performed by the female partner.

Marxist Theory of the Family: Zaretsky

Marxist sociologists argue that the family serves the interests of capitalism rather than society as a whole. Eli Zaretsky (1976) argued that the family under capitalism performs two key functions for the bourgeoisie. First, it reproduces the labour force — workers raise the next generation of workers at their own expense, subsidising capitalism’s need for a continuing workforce. Second, it acts as an emotional refuge: Parsons’s “warm bath” is, for Zaretsky, a mechanism that stabilises capitalism by absorbing workers’ discontent. Workers who experience alienation and exploitation at work are directed to seek fulfilment in family life, reducing the likelihood of collective resistance.

Zaretsky also argued that the family functions as a unit of consumption — purchasing the goods and services that generate profit for the bourgeoisie. The home filled with consumer goods (appliances, food, clothing, entertainment) represents a major market for capitalist industry. From this perspective, the cultural celebration of home and family life serves the interests of capitalism rather than genuinely meeting workers’ needs. The family also performs an ideological function: it presents existing social arrangements as natural and permanent, discouraging challenge to the capitalist order.

Christine Delphy and Diana Leonard developed a structural feminist critique of the family that went beyond individual men behaving badly. They argued that the family is best understood as a patriarchal economic institution — one in which the husband is the head and primary beneficiary of all work performed within the household. Women’s domestic labour — cooking, cleaning, child rearing, emotional support, nursing the sick — is systematically exploited by men, who benefit from these services without equivalent compensation. This is not a matter of individual relationships but of a structural arrangement in which men as a group benefit from women’s unpaid work.

Delphy and Leonard also argued that women’s position within the family keeps them economically dependent, reducing their capacity to challenge patriarchal arrangements. What Murdock called the “economic function” of the family is, from Delphy and Leonard’s perspective, a system in which women’s labour is extracted for men’s benefit under the guise of love and care.

Feminist Theory of the Family: Oakley

Ann Oakley challenged the functionalist picture from a feminist direction. She argued that the conventional family — with its gendered division of labour — is not a natural arrangement but a socially constructed one that disadvantages women. What Parsons presented as the “expressive role” is, in practice, unpaid domestic labour that women perform while men benefit from the financial returns of the “instrumental role”. Oakley’s concept of the double shift captures the additional burden on women who enter paid employment: rather than the domestic division of labour adjusting, women simply acquire a second shift of work on top of domestic responsibilities.

Key Fact

Three perspectives compete on the role of the family: functionalists (Parsons) see it as performing essential functions benefiting all of society; Marxists (Zaretsky) see it as serving capitalism by reproducing the workforce and absorbing discontent; feminists (Oakley; Delphy and Leonard) see it as serving men’s interests through women’s unpaid labour in a patriarchal structure.

New Right Theory of the Family

The New Right perspective, associated with Charles Murray, shares the functionalist view that the nuclear family is the most beneficial family form but adds a political critique of family change. Murray argued that the growth of lone parent families, cohabitation and family breakdown has contributed to the development of an underclass — a group dependent on state benefits, disconnected from mainstream society and passing this lifestyle on to the next generation. The New Right argues that the welfare state has inadvertently made it economically rational for women to raise children alone, removing the incentive for male responsibility within the family.

The New Right view is criticised by feminist sociologists, who argue it pathologises lone parent families without recognising the structural causes of their difficulties (poverty, the gender pay gap, lack of affordable child care). From a feminist perspective, the New Right’s concern is really about restoring male authority within the family rather than genuinely addressing poverty or social inequality.

A common error is treating the functions of the family as a neutral list that all perspectives accept. In fact, while Parsons describes the family’s functions positively (it meets real social needs), Marxists and feminists fundamentally challenge whose needs are being served. Feminists point out that the “expressive role” disguises unpaid female labour. Marxists argue the “economic function” involves reproducing the workforce and consuming capitalist products. The New Right endorses the functionalist picture but adds a political critique of state welfare. The same activities can be described very differently depending on which theoretical starting point you adopt — this is exactly the kind of perspectival comparison that earns marks in the 9-mark and 12-mark questions.
exam_tip_html:
On a 12-mark Evaluate question about theories of the family, the most common mistake is presenting only the functionalist view (Parsons) and stopping there. The mark scheme explicitly rewards candidates who present the functionalist case AND at least two contrasting perspectives. Name your sociologists precisely: “Zaretsky argued that…”, “Delphy and Leonard contended that…”, “Murray’s New Right view holds that…”. The conflict versus consensus debate is the structural frame your answer needs — always signal which side of the debate each sociologist falls on.

On a 2-mark Define question for “primary socialisation”, include two elements: (1) it is the earliest stage of socialisation and (2) it occurs within the family. Writing only “learning norms and values” without specifying the family as the agent earns 1 mark, not 2.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Parsons (functionalist) argued the family has two irreducible functions: primary socialisation and stabilisation of adult personalities (“warm bath” theory). The instrumental role (male breadwinner) and expressive role (female carer) are complementary and functionally necessary.
  • Zaretsky (Marxist) argued the family serves capitalism: it reproduces the workforce, absorbs worker discontent, acts as a unit of consumption and performs an ideological function. Delphy and Leonard and Oakley (feminist) argue the family serves men’s interests through women’s unpaid domestic labour in a patriarchal structure.
  • Murray’s New Right perspective views family diversity, particularly lone parent families, as contributing to an underclass and dependency culture. Feminist sociologists challenge this, arguing it pathologises lone parent families without addressing the structural causes of poverty.

practice_questions.text:
Which sociologist argued that the family serves capitalism by reproducing the workforce and absorbing worker discontent?
A) Talcott Parsons
B) Ann Oakley
C) Eli Zaretsky
D) Charles Murray

practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying it as the earliest/first stage of socialisation; 1 mark for explaining that it occurs within the family and involves children learning the basic norms and values of their society. Example: 'Primary socialisation is the earliest stage of socialisation, occurring within the family, through which children learn the basic norms and values of their society.'

practice_questions.text: Identify and describe one feminist criticism of the functionalist view of the family.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying a feminist criticism (e.g. the expressive role disguises unpaid domestic labour; the family serves men's interests not society's; the division of roles is patriarchal, not complementary). 2 marks for a developed description with a named feminist sociologist: e.g. 'Delphy and Leonard argued that the family is a patriarchal economic institution in which the husband is the head and chief beneficiary of all work performed within the household. Women's domestic labour — cooking, child care, emotional support — is systematically exploited for men's benefit. This means what Parsons described as the complementary expressive role is in practice a form of structural exploitation.'

practice_questions.text: Describe Zaretsky's Marxist view of the role of the family under capitalism.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks. 1 mark for naming Zaretsky and identifying the Marxist perspective. 1 mark for one function: the family reproduces the labour force, with workers raising the next generation of workers at their own expense, subsidising capitalism. 1 mark for a second function: the family absorbs worker discontent, acting as an emotional refuge that reduces the likelihood of collective resistance to capitalism. 1 mark for a further development: e.g. Zaretsky argued the family also acts as a unit of consumption, purchasing goods that generate profit for the bourgeoisie, and performs an ideological function by making capitalist social relations appear natural.

practice_questions.text: Discuss the view that the family benefits all its members equally.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Both sides of the debate developed with named sociologists, sociological vocabulary used accurately, a supported judgement. For (the family benefits all): Parsons's functionalist argument that the two irreducible functions (primary socialisation and personality stabilisation) benefit children, adults and society as a whole; the warm bath theory suggests both partners gain emotional stability. Against: Feminist view (Oakley; Delphy and Leonard) that the family primarily benefits men through women's unpaid labour; the double shift and triple shift show women bear disproportionate burdens; Marxist view (Zaretsky) that the family benefits the bourgeoisie rather than workers. New Right (Murray) argues traditional family benefits all, but implies some family forms are more beneficial than others. Supported conclusion that weighs which perspective is most convincing.

Secure: Both sides present, at least one named sociologist, judgement at the end.

Developing: Relevant points, mostly one-sided or undeveloped. Some named theorists. Conclusion assertive.

Emerging: Basic description, few named sociologists, little judgement.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the conflict versus consensus debate about the role of the family in society.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Full range of relevant arguments for and against, at least two named sociologists or perspectives developed in detail, sociological vocabulary used accurately, a clear supported judgement. Consensus (functionalist): Parsons's primary socialisation and warm bath theory; instrumental and expressive roles as complementary; the New Right's endorsement of the traditional nuclear family. Conflict perspectives: Marxist (Zaretsky) — the family serves capitalism, not society; reproduces the workforce, absorbs discontent, unit of consumption, ideological function; feminist (Delphy and Leonard) — the family is a patriarchal economic institution exploiting women's labour; Oakley's conventional family and double shift. Comparison of consensus and conflict claims: both identify 'functions' but disagree on who benefits. Sociological vocabulary (primary socialisation, instrumental role, patriarchy, bourgeoisie, ideological function, underclass, dependency culture) used accurately. Comparison and contrast of perspectives explicit. Substantiated conclusion that weighs the evidence.

Secure: Most relevant arguments present, both sides covered, named sociologists referenced, judgement present.

Developing: Relevant points but mostly one-sided or undeveloped. Some named theorists. Conclusion assertive.

Emerging: Basic points, mainly description, few or no named sociologists, little judgement.

knowledge_checks.q: Which perspective argues that the family is a patriarchal economic institution in which women's domestic labour is exploited for men's benefit?
Parsons argued that in modern industrial society the family performs two irreducible functions. Which of the following is one of them?
Zaretsky argued that the family serves _____ rather than society as a whole, by reproducing the workforce and absorbing worker discontent.
Parsons argued that in modern industrial society the family provides the stabilisation of adult personalities — sometimes called the _____ theory.
Match each sociologist to their key argument about the family:
right: The family performs primary socialisation and stabilises adult personalities
The family serves capitalism by reproducing the workforce and absorbing worker discontent
The family is a patriarchal economic institution in which women's labour is exploited for men's benefit

flashcard_questions.q: What are Parsons's two irreducible functions of the family?
flashcard_questions.a: Primary socialisation of children, and stabilisation of adult personalities.
The family provides emotional comfort that releases adults' work-related stress, stabilising their personalities.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the instrumental role in Parsons's theory?
flashcard_questions.a: The male breadwinner role focused on paid employment and financial provision for the family.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the expressive role in Parsons's theory?
flashcard_questions.a: The female nurturing role focused on the emotional wellbeing and socialisation of children.
The earliest stage of socialisation, occurring within the family, teaching children basic norms and values.

flashcard_questions.q: What did Zaretsky argue about the family and capitalism?
flashcard_questions.a: The family reproduces the workforce, absorbs worker discontent and acts as a unit of consumption, all serving capitalism.

flashcard_questions.q: What is an ideological function of the family, in the Marxist view?
flashcard_questions.a: A function that reproduces and justifies the existing class structure, making capitalism appear natural and inevitable.

flashcard_questions.q: What did Delphy and Leonard argue about women's work in the family?
flashcard_questions.a: Women's domestic labour is systematically exploited by men, who are the primary beneficiaries of a patriarchal institution.

flashcard_questions.q: What is Murray's New Right view of lone parent families?
flashcard_questions.a: They contribute to a dependency culture and the development of an underclass, linked to poverty and educational underachievement.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the conflict versus consensus debate about the family?
flashcard_questions.a: Functionalists (consensus) argue the family benefits everyone; Marxists and feminists (conflict) argue it benefits the powerful at others' expense.

glossary_terms.definition: The earliest stage of socialisation, occurring within the family, through which children learn the basic norms and values of their culture.
Parsons's argument that the family provides emotional comfort and psychological stability for adult members, releasing tensions accumulated in paid work.
In Marxist theory, a function that serves to reproduce and justify the existing class structure, making capitalism appear natural and inevitable.
A system in which men hold structural power and women are systematically disadvantaged across social institutions including the family.
In Marxist theory, the class that owns the means of production and employs others for profit.
Murray's New Right term for a group at the bottom of the class structure characterised by welfare dependency and a rejection of mainstream values.
A sociological approach, such as functionalism, that views society as characterised by shared values and institutions working for the benefit of all.
A sociological approach, such as Marxism or feminism, that views society as characterised by inequality and conflict between groups with different interests.

hero_image_caption: Competing sociological perspectives offer contrasting views of the family's role in society.
